## The Essence of the Great Parashara Horoscopy

> Having heard this entire science of horoscopy <term>horā-śāstra</term> with faith and humility ||
> directly from the mouth of a teacher <note>original: "guru-mukhāt"</note>, and having reflected upon it with intelligence || 1 ||
> He who truly understands the meaning of the scriptures is liberated from all sins ||
> The wise one should then teach it and show it to others, becoming like a second Garga <note>A legendary sage and one of the founding fathers of Indian astronomy/astrology</note>, best among the twice-born || 2 ||

---

**Commentary**—Having bowed to Lord Ganesha, I now compose a commentary on the twentieth [chapter] according to my ability. I explain here the fruits of the science and the lineage of the science's tradition. || 1 || In this twentieth chapter, the venerable Great Sage <note>Maharishi Parashara</note> speaks about the results of the science and the tradition of the science in a chapter consisting of five verses. In the first two and a half verses, he describes the results. This entire science of horoscopy <term>horā-śāstra</term> mentioned by me [should be approached] with faith and humility. Faith <note>original: "śraddhā"</note> consists of trust in the words of the teacher and the scripture. Humility <note>original: "vinaya"</note> means a state of devotion toward teachers and elders. One should hear the meaning of this science "from the mouth of a teacher" and not merely on one's own. The wise student, having heard and then "observed"—meaning having personally and thoroughly reflected upon it—knows the meaning of this science. Such a person becomes all-knowing through the power of the teacher and the scripture. Furthermore, there is another result: "he is liberated from all sins." Thereafter, being a qualified authority, he should "teach and show" it to others. If a doubt is raised that "star-gazers" <note>astrologers</note> are described by lawgivers like Manu as being flawed and thus ineligible to be invited to ancestral feasts <term>śrāddha</term>, and therefore there might be a suspicion of sin attached to this profession, the author shows the highest state for the knower of this science to dispel that doubt: "He goes to the World of Brahma" <term>brahmaloka</term>. || 1 || 2 ||

**Vernacular Translation**—Now the results and the tradition of the science are stated. One should study this science of horoscopy <term>horā-śāstra</term> that I have taught from the mouth of a teacher and reflect upon it; then true knowledge will arise. Afterwards, through the influence of the teacher and the scripture, one will become all-knowing and be freed from sin. One should then allow other virtuous people to hear and see this knowledge. Through the perfect knowledge of this science, one goes to the World of Brahma <note>The highest heaven or state of ultimate reality</note>. || 1 || 2 ||

> Completely freed from all sins, he goes to the World of Brahma ||
> Having extracted it from the Vedas, Brahma spoke it in great detail || 3 ||
> This very science is the primordial one, a limb of the Vedas <term>vedāṅga</term> and the "Eyes of the Vedas" <note>The Vedas are the oldest sacred texts of India; Jyotisha or astrology is considered the "eye" because it allows one to see the correct time for rituals and the workings of karma</note> ||

<meta>Footer: CC-0 Shri Krishna Museum, Kurukshetra. Digitized by eGangotri</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the spiritual rewards of studying astrology, asserting that a student who learns with humility from a teacher is freed from sin and attains the highest spiritual realm. It also defends the purity of the astrological profession and traces the science's origin back to the creator-god Brahma as a vital "limb" of the Vedas.</summary>

<keywords>horoscopy, Parashara, Brahma, teacher-disciple tradition, liberation, Vedas, Vedanga, sin, Garga, astrology</keywords>

<page-num>767</page-num>

# In the Latter Section, Chapter 20: Description of the Results of Study

**Commentary**—One might raise an objection: Is the promise of attaining the World of Brahma <note>original: "Brahmaloka," the highest heaven or state of existence</note> through the acceptance of this scripture merely a form of figurative praise <note>original: "arthavāda," a rhetorical exaggeration used to encourage practice</note>? Does it lack the specific merit seen in reciting the Vedas since it is a man-made composition? 

The author answers "No" in the next two half-verses. The Creator Brahma extracted this primary science from the Vedas, where it was explained in detail, and spoke it to the sage Garga. If one asks how a work by Parashara can be called "primary," it is because it is a <term>Vedānga</term> <note>A "Limb of the Veda," one of the six auxiliary disciplines used to understand and apply Vedic knowledge</note>. The implication is that one should not doubt this as a mere human invention. 

If one asks which specific part of the Veda this represents, the text replies that it is the <term>Veda-cakṣu</term> <note>The "Eye of the Veda"</note>. As stated in the *Shiksha* <note>The Vedic study of phonetics</note>: "Astronomy/Astrology is the eye of the sacrifice." Among all the limbs of the body, the eye possesses the power of specific knowledge; because this science holds that position, it generates specialized knowledge and is therefore supreme. Consequently, the statement that studying this leads to the World of Brahma—just like studying the Vedas—is literal truth and not mere praise. || 3 ||

**Translation**—In ancient times, the Creator Brahma extracted this primary science of <term>Jyotisha</term> <note>The traditional Indian system of astrology and astronomy</note> from the Vedas and taught it to the sage Garga. This science is the "eye" limb of the Veda. || 3 ||

->Garga spoke this to me, and I have spoken it to you exactly as it is. || 4 ||<-
->Thus, the science has been told to you, Maitreya, from its beginning to its very end. || 5 ||<-

## Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Results of the Study," 
## in the Latter Section of the Great Parashara Horoscopy. || 20 ||

**Commentary**—Now he describes the lineage of the tradition. The sage Garga, having understood this science from the Creator Brahma, spoke it to me [Parashara]. I, too, have told you everything from the beginning to the end, exactly as I learned it from Garga. This is stated with certainty. || 4 || 5 || 

<term>In this latter half of the Great Parashara Horoscopy</term>, this commentary has been composed according to my limited intelligence; may it be an offering to Lord Ganesha. || 1 || From the sages... <note>original: "ārṣamā-," a catchword indicating the start of the next section or page</note>

<summary>This concluding page establishes the divine authority of the horoscopic science, tracing its lineage from the god Brahma to the sage Garga and finally to Parashara. It asserts that astrology is the "Eye of the Veda" and that its study grants the same spiritual rewards as the Vedas themselves.</summary>

<keywords>Brahmaloka, Garga, Parashara, Vedanga, Jyotisha, Veda-cakshu, Maitreya, lineage, divine origin</keywords>

# Summary of the Great Parashara Horoscopy

This science is easy to understand and contains a vast collection of knowledge. Seeing it falling into a state of loss, I was moved by the desire to bring it back into use. || 2 || 

Wandering through many different lands over several years, I gathered whatever portions I could obtain from various places. || 3 || 

Taking those gathered parts, this book has been edited and prepared by me. I have also composed a commentary <note>The "Subodhini" commentary</note> here, relying on the wisdom of the learned to the best of my own ability. || 4 || 

Due to the unavailability of many manuscripts and the negligence of various scribes, even in this edition—to the extent that my own intellectual strength allowed— || 5 || 

I have performed corrections and written this commentary. Whatever is missing or excessive here, I ask all scholars to kindly forgive and correct it. || 6 ||

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Declaration of the Results of Study," in the *Subodhini* <note>Meaning "That which explains well"</note> commentary. This was composed by the illustrious astrologer Shridhara, son of the astrologer Jatashankara, of the flawless lineage of Dadhyang <note>A lineage tracing back to the Vedic sage Dadhichi</note>, who has illuminated all directions with his knowledge of the Vedas and other sciences. He was assisted by Shri Krishna Sahaya of the Dhaureya family. This concludes the Latter Section of the *Great Parashara Horoscopy*. || 20 ||

**Vernacular Summary**—Sage Garga, having studied this science under the Creator Brahma, later recounted it to me. O Maitreya! I have now told you this entire science from beginning to end. || 4 || 5 ||

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Declaration of the Results of Study," in the vernacular commentary on the Latter Section of the *Great Parashara Horoscopy*. It was composed by the astrologer Shridhara, son of Jatashankara, of the illustrious Dadhyang lineage, with the assistance of Harikrishna Sahaya, son of the astrologer Devarama. || 20 ||

---

->And this book is finished.<-

*   **The Great Compendium:** The term <term>Bṛhat</term> translates to "great," "vast," or "extensive." It signifies that this is not a mere summary, but a comprehensive encyclopedic treatment of the subject.
*   **Sage Parashara:** The work is attributed to the ancient sage <term>Parāśara</term>. In the Vedic tradition, Parashara is a semi-legendary figure, the grandson of Vashistha and the father of Vyasa (the compiler of the Vedas). He is revered as the supreme authority on the rules of planetary influence.
*   **The Science of Time:** The word <term>Horā</term> refers to the study of time, specifically horoscopy and the calculation of auspicious moments. <term>Śāstra</term> denotes a formal science, treatise, or body of knowledge. Together, they describe a rigorous system for understanding how celestial movements correspond to human destiny.

*   **Shastra**: Meaning "Science," "Treatise," or "Sacred Teaching." It denotes a systematic body of knowledge that is both authoritative and instructional.

# Science of Horoscopy
<note>original: Bṛhatpārāśarahorā-śāstram</note>

<note>The central paper label is torn at the upper right corner. Significant dark staining or water damage is visible on the lower half of the textured red cover.</note>

->**The Title Label**<-

The decorative label on the cover identifies this manuscript as the <term>Bṛhatpārāśarahorā-śāstram</term>, the primary foundational scripture of <term>Indian Astrology (Jyotiṣa)</term>. 

*   **Great (Bṛhat):** This indicates that the text is the "large" or comprehensive version of the astrological teachings.
*   **Parashara’s (Pārāśara):** The work is attributed to the ancient <term>Rishi Parashara</term>, a semi-legendary sage and father of the author of the Mahabharata, regarded as the primary authority on Indian horoscopy.
*   **Horoscopy (Horā):** This term refers to the study of time, specifically the science of casting and interpreting birth charts. It is traditionally considered a derivative of the Sanskrit word for "day and night" <note>original: ahorātra</note>.
*   **Science (Śāstram):** This denotes an authoritative, systematic body of knowledge, a sacred treatise, or a technical manual.

<note>The label is framed by a decorative geometric and floral border, a style common in the bookbinding of the late 19th and early 20th centuries in South Asia.</note>

*   **Science** <note>original: Śāstra</note>: A systematic, authoritative body of knowledge or a sacred treatise.

This title page introduces the <term>Bṛhat Pārāśara Horā Śāstra</term> <note>often simply called the BPHS</note>, the most vital and comprehensive treatise in the tradition of <term>Jyotiṣa</term> <note>the traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology</note>.

The title carries deep significance:
*   **Great** <note>original: Bṛhat</note>: Denotes the vast, encyclopedic nature of this specific version of the text.
*   **Of Parashara** <note>original: Pārāśara</note>: Attributes the teachings to the sage Parashara, a legendary figure in Vedic literature and the father of Vyasa.
*   **Horoscopy** <note>original: Horā</note>: Refers to the study of time, specifically birth charts and the influence of celestial bodies on human life.
*   **Science** <note>original: Śāstra</note>: Defines the work as a systematic, authoritative body of sacred knowledge.

This specific copy, held at the Shri Krishna Museum in Kurukshetra, represents the enduring legacy of ancient Indian mathematical and celestial observation. Despite the physical damage to the cover and the staining on the binding, the bold Devanagari calligraphy remains clear, inviting the reader into the complex calculations and spiritual insights of the Parashara school of astrology.

This work is universally regarded as the foundational and most authoritative text in the field of <term>Indian Astrology</term> <note>original: Jyotiṣa; the traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology</note>.

The components of the title illustrate the manuscript's significance:

*   **Great** <note>original: Bṛhat</note>: This prefix distinguishes this comprehensive, encyclopedic version from shorter or abridged versions.
*   **Parashara’s** <note>original: Pārāśara</note>: Named for the ancient sage Parashara, who, according to tradition, received this celestial knowledge from the creator and passed it to his disciple Maitreya.
*   **Horoscopy** <note>original: Horā</note>: A term referring to the study of time, specifically the casting of horoscopes based on the hour of birth.
*   **Science** <note>original: Śāstra</note>: A technical term for a sacred treatise or a formal system of knowledge.

This work is the foundational text of **Vedic Astrology** <term>Jyotiṣa</term> <note>literally "the science of light," referring to the study of celestial bodies</note>.

The title identifies the text through four key Sanskrit concepts:

*   **Great** <note>original: Bṛhat</note>: This indicates the text is a comprehensive or "expanded" version, distinguishing it from shorter or abridged manuals.
*   **Parashara’s** <note>original: Pārāśara</note>: This attributes the authorship to the ancient sage Parashara, who is traditionally regarded as the father of Indian astrology.
*   **Horoscopy** <note>original: Horā</note>: A technical term for the branch of astrology focused on time, specifically the interpretation of birth charts and planetary hours.
*   **Science** <note>original: Śāstram</note>: This signifies that the work is a systematic, authoritative treatise or a body of sacred knowledge.

The text presented here is **The Great Compendium of Parashara’s Science of Horoscopy** <note>original Sanskrit title: Bṛhatpārāśarahorāśāstram</note>. This work is widely regarded as the most authoritative and comprehensive foundational treatise in the field of **Indian Astrology** <term>Jyotisha: the traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology, literally meaning "the science of light"</term>.

The title is composed of four essential elements that define its status:

*   **Great** <note>original: Bṛhat</note>: This prefix signifies that the work is an expansive or "major" version of the teachings, indicating its status as a complete and exhaustive authority compared to smaller summaries.
*   **Parashara’s** <note>original: Pārāśara</note>: The text is attributed to the ancient sage Parashara. In the Vedic tradition, he is a highly revered seer, the grandson of the sage Vashistha, and the father of Vyasa <note>the traditional author of the Great Epic, the Mahabharata</note>.
*   **Horoscopy** <note>original: Horā</note>: This refers to the specific branch of astrology dealing with time, particularly the interpretation of birth charts and the influence of planets on human destiny.
*   **Science** <note>original: Śāstram</note>: This term identifies the work as a systematic body of knowledge, a formal treatise, or a sacred manual of rules and laws.

# The Great Compendium of-
# Parashara’s Science of Horoscopy.

<margin>The central label is torn at the upper right corner and features a decorative floral and geometric border.</margin>

The text presented here is **The Great Compendium of Parashara’s Science of Horoscopy** <note>original Sanskrit title: Bṛhatpārāśarahorāśāstram</note>. This work is widely regarded as the most authoritative and comprehensive foundational treatise in the field of **Indian Astrology** <term>Jyotisha: the traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology, literally meaning "the science of light"</term>.

The title is composed of four essential elements that define its status:

*   **Great** <note>original: Bṛhat</note>: This prefix signifies that the work is an expansive or "major" version of the teachings, indicating its status as a complete and exhaustive authority compared to smaller or condensed summaries.
*   **Parashara’s** <note>original: Pārāśara</note>: The text is attributed to the ancient sage Parashara. In the Vedic tradition, he is a highly revered seer, the grandson of the sage Vashistha, and the father of Vyasa <note>the legendary author of the Great Epic, the Mahabharata</note>.
*   **Horoscopy** <note>original: Horā</note>: This refers to the specific branch of astrology dealing with time, particularly the interpretation of birth charts and the influence of planetary movements on human destiny.
*   **Science** <note>original: Śāstram</note>: This term identifies the work as a systematized, authoritative body of knowledge or a formal treatise intended to be studied as a sacred discipline.

* <gloss>Great, Extensive, or Comprehensive</gloss> <note>original Sanskrit: Bṛhat</note> — this indicates that the manuscript is a major or complete version of the text, rather than an abridgment.
* <gloss>of the sage Parashara</gloss> <note>original Sanskrit: Pārāśara</note> — this attributes the lineage of the knowledge to one of the "great seers" of ancient India.
* <gloss>Astrology or Horoscopy</gloss> <note>original Sanskrit: Horā</note> — this refers specifically to the branch of knowledge concerned with the interpretation of time and the influence of celestial bodies on human life.
* <gloss>Science, Treatise, or Sacred Manual</gloss> <note>original Sanskrit: Śāstram</note> — this denotes that the text is a formal, systematized, and authoritative body of knowledge.

# The Great Compendium of Parashara’s-
# Astrological Science.

<margin>The central paper label is pasted onto a red book cover; the label is torn at the upper right corner. Dark stains and significant wear are visible on the surrounding red fabric.</margin>

->**The Great Compendium of Parashara’s-**<-
->**Astrological Science.**<-

<term>The Great Compendium (original: Bṛhat)</term>: This Sanskrit prefix translates to "large," "great," or "vast." In traditional Indian literature, it indicates that the text is the comprehensive or major version of a teaching, distinguishing it from shorter summaries.

<term>Parashara (original: Pārāśara)</term>: Refers to the legendary sage (Maharishi) Parashara, who is traditionally credited as the author of this work. He is a central figure in Vedic genealogy, regarded as the grandson of Vashistha and the father of Vyasa, the compiler of the Vedas.

<term>Astrological Science (original: Horā-śāstra)</term>: A technical term for the study of time and planetary influence. *Horā* refers to the branch of astrology dealing with individual horoscopes and the passage of hours (a word with which it shares an ancient root), while *śāstra* denotes an authoritative scientific or sacred treatise.

<note>The title identifies the *Bṛhat Pārāśara Horā Śāstra*, which is considered the foundational "bible" of Indian predictive astrology (Jyotisha). Most modern systems of Indian natal astrology are derived from the principles laid out in this specific compendium.</note>

He is a towering figure in Vedic literature, regarded as the father of the sage Vyasa (the compiler of the Vedas) and the primary authority on ancient Indian horoscopy.

<term>Astrological Science</term> <note>original: "Horā-śāstram" (होराशास्त्रम्)</note>: A systematic treatise (*śāstra*) concerning the science of time and horoscopy (*horā*). The term *horā* is thought to be derived from *ahorātra* (day and night). This discipline focuses on the birth charts of individuals and the celestial influences governing their lives.

<term>Horoscopy</term> <note>original: "Horā" (होरा)</note>: The specific branch of astrology focused on birth charts and the influence of time on human life. Etymologically, it is said to be derived from the Sanskrit word for "day and night" <note>original: "ahorātra" (अहोरात्र)</note>, signifying the passage of time.

<term>Treatise</term> <note>original: "Śāstra" (शास्त्रम्)</note>: A systematic body of knowledge, science, or a formal manual of instruction. It implies that the content follows a logical, traditional methodology rather than being a collection of folklore.

<term>Treatise</term> <note>original: "Shastram" (शास्त्रम्). A word denoting a formal, systematic body of knowledge or a sacred secular text that provides rules and instructions on a specific science or art.</note>

<term>Great Compendium</term> <note>original: "Bṛhat" (वृहत्). In the Sanskrit tradition, this signifies an expansive, foundational, or "great" work, distinguishing this comprehensive text from shorter or abridged manuals on the same subject.</note>

<term>Parashara</term> <note>original: "Pārāśara" (पाराशर). This identifies the work as belonging to the lineage of the Sage Parashara. In Vedic tradition, he is a revered seer and the father of Vyasa (the author of the Mahabharata). He is considered the primary authority on the system of astrology detailed in this volume.</note>

<term>Science of Horoscopy</term> <note>original: "Horā-śāstram" (होरा-शास्त्रम्). This is a technical term for predictive astrology. "Hora" refers to the study of time and the rising sign of the zodiac, while "Shastra" denotes a systematic, authoritative treatise or sacred science.</note>

<margin>The physical object is a book bound in a deep red, textured material. At its center is a rectangular paper label, now yellowed, featuring the title printed in Devanagari script. <note>The label is slightly damaged, with a visible tear at the upper right corner. Several dark smudges and stains are scattered across the lower half of the red cover, likely from handling or age.</note></margin>

<note>The title label is enclosed in an ornamental border with repeating floral or geometric patterns. This style of framing is characteristic of lithographed books and early printed Sanskrit editions from the late 19th or early 20th centuries in India.</note>

<term>Great Compendium</term> <note>original: "Bṛhat" (बृहत्). In Sanskrit literature, this prefix indicates a comprehensive or "large" version of a foundational text, distinguishing it from shorter summaries or specialized manuals.</note>

<term>Parashara’s</term> <note>original: "Pārāśara" (पाराशर). This refers to the Sage Parashara, who is traditionally honored as the father of Indian astrology (Jyotisha) and the primary author of this system.</note>

<term>Science of Astrology</term> <note>original: "Horā-śāstram" (होरा-शास्त्रम्). "Hora" refers to the study of time, zodiac signs, and the prediction of destiny; "Shastra" refers to an authoritative, systematic body of knowledge or a sacred treatise.</note>

<note>A modern digital watermark at the bottom edge of the image identifies the source as the Shri Krishna Museum, Kurukshetra, digitized by the eGangotri initiative. The text "CC-0" indicates it is in the public domain.</note>

<term>The Great Science of Parashara’s Astrology</term> <note>original: "Bṛhat Pārāśara Horā-śāstram" (बृहत्पाराशरहोरा-शास्त्रम्). This is the definitive foundational text of Indian predictive astrology (Jyotisha). "Bṛhat" (बृहत्) means "great" or "comprehensive." "Pārāśara" (पाराशर) refers to the legendary sage Parashara, the traditional author. "Horā" (होरा) is a technical term for horoscopic or natal astrology, derived from the study of planetary hours. "Śāstra" (शास्त्रम्) denotes a systematic, authoritative scientific treatise.</note>

This specific manuscript is part of the collection at the Shri Krishna Museum in Kurukshetra and has been digitized for public heritage access.</note>

# The Great Science of
# Parashara’s Astrology. <unclear>1/2</unclear>

<term>The Great Science of Parashara’s Astrology</term> <note>original: "Bṛhat Pārāśara Horā-śāstram" (बृहत्पाराशरहोरा-शास्त्रम्). This is the definitive foundational text of Indian predictive astrology, known as Jyotisha. "Bṛhat" (बृहत्) means "great" or "comprehensive," indicating the encyclopedic nature of the work. "Pārāśara" (पाराशर) refers to the legendary sage Parashara, who is the traditional author and father of Vyasa. "Horā" (होरा) is a technical term for horoscopic or natal astrology, traditionally said to be derived from the Sanskrit word "Ahoratra" (day and night) by dropping the first and last syllables. "Śāstra" (शास्त्रम्) denotes a systematic, authoritative scientific treatise or body of knowledge.</note>

<note>Artistic Detail: The title is framed by a decorative printed border featuring an ornamental floral pattern, typical of late 19th or early 20th-century Indian book production. The label is pasted onto a red cloth-textured cover. This manuscript is held in the collection of the Shri Krishna Museum and has been preserved through the eGangotri digitization initiative.</note>

<summary>This page features the front cover and title label for the "Bṛhat Pārāśara Horāśāstra," the most influential and authoritative text in the tradition of Indian predictive astrology attributed to the sage Parashara.</summary>

# The Great Compendium of Parashara’s Horoscopy-
# Science. <unclear>⌇</unclear>

<term>The Great Compendium of Parashara’s Horoscopy-Science</term> <note>original Sanskrit: *Bṛhat-Pārāśara-Horā-Śāstram*. This is considered the most authoritative and comprehensive foundational text of Indian predictive astrology (<term>Jyotiṣa</term>). It is traditionally attributed to the Vedic sage Parashara, who is a central figure in ancient Indian literature and the father of the sage Vyasa, the compiler of the Vedas.</note>

<note>The term <term>Horā</term> refers to the branch of astrology dealing with individual horoscopes and the passage of time. Etymologically, it is often associated with the Greek word *hōra* (hour). The word <term>Śāstram</term> denotes a systematic, scientific, or sacred treatise that provides authoritative instruction. Together, they represent a "Science of Time" used to interpret destiny based on the positions of celestial bodies at the moment of birth.</note>

It is traditionally credited to the sage Parashara, who is said to have revealed this knowledge at the beginning of our current cosmic age, the Kali Yuga.</term>

# The Great Compendium of Parashara’s
# Science of Horoscopy.

<note>original: "बृहत्पाराशरहोराशास्त्रम्" (Bṛhatpārāśarahorāśāstram)</note>

<note>The manuscript begins with this formal title page. The text is written in the Devanagari script, the standard script for Sanskrit. This specific edition is preserved in the Shri Krishna Museum collection. The title indicates that this is the "Great" (Bṛhat) version of the text, suggesting a comprehensive or expanded collection of the sage’s teachings.</note>

<term>Bṛhat: Meaning "great," "large," or "vast." In the context of Sanskrit literature, it often denotes a comprehensive or definitive version of a text.</term>

<term>Pārāśara: Refers to the Sage Parāśara, a prominent figure in Vedic literature. He is considered the father of the sage Vyāsa (who compiled the Vedas) and the primary authority on this system of astrology.</term>

<term>Horā: Derived from the Sanskrit root for "time," this term refers specifically to predictive astrology or horoscopy. It is the study of the influence of celestial bodies on human life based on the time of birth.</term>

<term>Śāstra: A systematic treatise or scientific work. Calling this work a "shastra" indicates its status as an authoritative and structured body of knowledge.</term>

<term>Jyotiṣa: The broader Vedic science of astronomy and astrology, of which "Horā" is a principal branch.</term>

<term>Śāstra: A systematic treatise, science, or body of knowledge. It implies the text is an authoritative instructional manual.</term>

<term>Jyotiṣa: The traditional Vedic system of astronomy and astrology, of which this text is considered the cornerstone.</term>

# The Great Compendium of Parashara’s
# Science of Horoscopy.

<note>original: "बृहत्पाराशरहोराशास्त्रम्" (Bṛhatpārāśarahorāśāstram)</note>

<note>The central title label is displayed within a decorative label featuring a floral border pattern. The label is torn at the upper-right corner, and there are significant dark stains or ink blotches on the lower half of the red cover cloth, indicating extensive historical use.</note>

<term>Bṛhatpārāśarahorāśāstra: The "Great Compendium of Parashara’s Science of Horoscopy." This is the foundational and most comprehensive text of <term>Jyotiṣa</term> (traditional Indian astrology).</term>

<term>Parāśara: An ancient Vedic sage (Rishi) regarded as the father of this specific school of astrology. In Hindu tradition, he is also known as the father of Vyasa, the legendary author of the Mahabharata.</term>

<term>Horā: A term referring to the science of time or "horoscopy," specifically the branch of astrology dealing with individual horoscopes and predictions.</term>

<term>Śāstra: An authoritative treatise, scientific manual, or a sacred body of knowledge in the Sanskrit tradition.</term>

<term>Jyotiṣa: The traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology, often translated as "the science of light" or "the study of heavenly bodies."</term>

# The Great Treatise of Parashara
# on the Science of Time.

<note>original: "वृहत्पाराशरहोराशास्त्रम्" (Bṛhat Pārāśara Horā Śāstram)</note>

<term>Bṛhat: A Sanskrit term meaning "great," "large," or "vast." When applied to a book, it indicates that this is the comprehensive or expanded version of a traditional teaching.</term>

<term>Pārāśara: Belonging to Parashara, a legendary sage and the father of Vyasa. He is revered as the primary authority in the system of astrology presented in this text.</term>

<term>Horā: Derived from the Sanskrit word for "hour," this term refers specifically to horoscopy or the branch of astrology focused on the zodiac, birth charts, and the passage of time.</term>

<term>Śāstra: A formal manual, treatise, or scientific textbook that provides authoritative rules on a specific discipline.</term>

<note>This text, the *Bṛhat Pārāśara Horā Śāstra*, is considered the foundational "bible" of Vedic astrology. It contains the rules for calculating planetary positions and interpreting their effects on human life, structured as a dialogue between the sage Parashara and his disciple Maitreya.</note>

<term>The Great Compendium of Parashara’s Astrology</term>: This is the standard title for the most influential text in Indian astrology. It is regarded as the primary source for the <term>Jyotisha</term> (Vedic astrology) system used for centuries to calculate birth charts and predict life events. <note>original Sanskrit: Bṛhatpārāśarahorāśāstram</note>

<term>Great</term> (<italic>Bṛhat</italic>): This prefix indicates that the work is a comprehensive or "large" version of the teachings, distinguishing it from shorter summaries or abridged versions of the same system.

<term>Parashara</term>: A celebrated sage in Hindu tradition. He is considered the grandson of the sage Vashistha and the father of Vyasa, the legendary compiler of the Vedas. Parashara is traditionally viewed as the original narrator of this astrological knowledge.

<term>Astrology</term> (<italic>Horā</italic>): Specifically refers to the branch of astrology dealing with hours, time, and the interpretation of individual birth charts (horoscopy). 

<term>Treatise</term> (<italic>Śāstra</italic>): A technical or scientific work of authority that provides systematic rules and knowledge on a specific subject.

## The Great Compendium of
## Parashara’s Astrology

<term>The Great Compendium of Parashara’s Astrology</term>: This is the formal title of the foundational text of <term>Indian Astrology</term> (known as <italic>Jyotisha</italic>). It is considered the most authoritative source for calculating planetary positions and interpreting birth charts in the Hindu tradition. <note>original Sanskrit: Bṛhatpārāśarahorāśāstram</note>

<term>Great</term> (<italic>Bṛhat</italic>): This prefix signifies that this is the comprehensive or "large" version of the teachings, distinguishing it from shorter summaries or abridgments.

<term>Parashara</term>: A revered sage in Indian history, known as the grandson of Vashistha and the father of Vyasa (the compiler of the Great Epic, the Mahabharata). He is the traditional narrator who revealed this astrological wisdom to his disciple Maitreya.

<term>Astrology</term> (<italic>Horā</italic>): This term specifically refers to the branch of astrology concerned with time and the prediction of an individual's life path through their horoscope. It shares an ancient linguistic root with the Greek word for "hour."

<term>Treatise</term> (<italic>Śāstra</italic>): A technical or scientific scripture that provides systematic rules and authoritative knowledge on a specialized subject.

***

->This title is printed on a rectangular paper label with a decorative floral border, centered on a red, textured book cover.<-

The paper has yellowed with age and is slightly torn at the top right corner. Dark stains, possibly from water or frequent handling, are visible on the lower half of the cover.</note>

# ASTROLOGICAL TREATISE.

<note>original Sanskrit: Bṛhatpārāśarahorāśāstram</note>

This label identifies the manuscript as <term>The Great Parashara Astrological Treatise</term> (known in Sanskrit as the *Brihat Parashara Hora Shastra*). It is considered the foundational and most influential text of <term>Vedic Astrology</term> (<italic>Jyotiṣa</italic>), the traditional Indian system of astronomy, time-keeping, and divination.

The title is composed of four significant parts:

**Great** (<italic>Bṛhat</italic>): This prefix indicates that the volume is a "large" or comprehensive compendium. It distinguishes this work from shorter, condensed summaries or "minor" (<italic>Laghu</italic>) versions within the same tradition.

**Parashara**: This refers to Sage Parashara, the legendary author. In Indian tradition, Parashara is a highly revered Vedic seer and the father of Vyasa (the narrator of the great epic <italic>Mahābhārata</italic>). He is regarded as the primary authority on the laws of destiny and the celestial influence of the planets.

**Horoscopy** (<term>Horā</term>): This term identifies the specific branch of astrology focused on birth charts, the determination of auspicious moments, and the measurement of time. <note>original: "horā"; Etymologically, scholars believe the Sanskrit word shares a root with the Ancient Greek "hōra," which is the origin of the English word "hour."</note>

**Treatise** (<term>Śāstra</term>): This indicates an authoritative, systematic body of knowledge or a scientific work. A <italic>Śāstra</italic> is not merely a book but a set of rules and principles that govern a specific field of study.

The title label, centered on the red textured cover, is enclosed within a decorative floral and geometric border typical of early 20th-century Indian book production. Although the paper label is slightly torn at the top right corner, the formal Devanagari script remains clearly readable.

*   **Shastra** <note>an "Authoritative Treatise" or "Sacred Manual"</note>

*   **Brihat**: Meaning "Great" or "Extensive," indicating the comprehensive nature of this collection.
*   **Parashara**: The name of the ancient Vedic sage; he is traditionally regarded as the father of Vyasa and the author of this astrological system.
*   **Hora**: The science of "Time," specifically referring to horoscopy and the measurement of planetary movements.
*   **Shastra**: A "Treatise," "Scripture," or sacred manual of specialized knowledge.

This foundational text provides the mathematical rules and philosophical principles used to interpret celestial positions, forming the basis for much of Indian astrological practice today.

# Horoscopic Astrology

This text is the most significant and foundational work in the tradition of <term>Vedic Astrology</term> <note>original: Jyotiṣa</note>. 

The volume is bound in a red textured cover. The title itself is printed in the <term>Devanagari</term> script—the standard script for Sanskrit—on a rectangular paper label.

<note>The label is damaged at the top right corner, and prominent dark stains or ink blotches are visible on the bottom half of the cover, reflecting its history and age.</note>

->The Decorative Border<-

The title is enclosed within a decorative border featuring floral fleuron patterns. This typographic style was common for book labels in the 19th and early 20th centuries, marking the work as a significant scholarly or religious text.

The work is attributed to the sage Parashara, a legendary figure often called the "father of horoscopy," who systematized the principles of how celestial bodies influence human life.

- **The Great Parashara Horoscopic** <note>Bṛhat-Pārāśara-Horā-</note>
- **Treatise** <note>Śāstram</note>

# The Great Compendium of Parashara’s
## Horoscopic Treatise

This central label identifies the text as the <term>Great Treatise on Parashara’s Horoscopy</term> <note>Sanskrit: Bṛhat Pārāśara Horāśāstra</note>. 

Within the vast tradition of <term>Vedic Astrology</term> <note>Jyotiṣa</note>, this work stands as the foundational authority for natal horoscopy. It is traditionally attributed to the ancient sage <term>Parashara</term>, who, according to legend, revealed these celestial secrets to his disciple Maitreya at the beginning of the current cosmic age, the Kali Yuga. 

The title is composed of several key Sanskrit concepts:
*   **The Great** <note>Bṛhat</note>: Indicating the comprehensive or "large" version of the text.
*   **Parashara** <note>Pārāśara</note>: The name of the sage to whom the knowledge is attributed.
*   **Horoscopic** <note>Horā</note>: A term for astrology that specifically concerns the rising sign and the study of hours.
*   **Treatise** <note>Śāstram</note>: A systematic, authoritative scripture or scientific work.

<note>The label is printed on a rectangular paper slip with a decorative floral border. The background of the book cover is a vibrant red with a subtle, repeating diamond-shaped geometric pattern. The physical condition of this specific copy shows damage to the upper right corner of the label and dark smudges on the lower half, indicating its history of use and preservation.</note>

# The Great Compendium of Parashara’s-
# Horoscopic Science.

<note>original Sanskrit: Bṛhatpārāśarahorāśāstram</note>

The label on this red, textured cover identifies the manuscript as the <term>Great Compendium of Parashara’s Horoscopic Science</term>. Within the tradition of <term>Vedic Astrology</term> <note>original: Jyotiṣa</note>, this work is revered as the most authoritative and comprehensive manual for calculating and interpreting the influence of stars and planets on human life.

The title breaks down into four significant Sanskrit components:
*   **The Great** <note>original: Bṛhat</note>: This signifies that the volume is an extensive or "great" collection of knowledge, distinguished from shorter summaries.
*   **Parashara** <note>original: Pārāśara</note>: This refers to the legendary Vedic sage Parashara, the traditional author of the text and a central figure in ancient Indian philosophy.

# The Great Treatise on

<note>original Sanskrit: "Bṛhatpārāśarahorāśāstram"</note>

This title introduces the foundational text of <term>Vedic Astrology</term> <note>Sanskrit: Jyotiṣa; the ancient Indian system of astronomy and time-keeping</note>. The work is traditionally attributed to the sage Parashara, a legendary figure of the Vedic era.

This page displays the formal title of one of the most significant works in the Indian tradition of astral science. The text, known as the <term>Bṛhat Pārāśara Horāśāstra</term>, is the foundational compendium for <term>Vedic Astrology</term> <note>original Sanskrit: Jyotiṣa</note>. 

The title consists of four key parts:
*   **Great** <note>original: Bṛhat</note> — This prefix suggests the work is an expansive, "great," or "large" version of the teachings.
*   **Of Parashara** <note>original: Pārāśara</note> — This attributes the text to the legendary sage Parashara, who is traditionally regarded as the father of the great sage Vyasa (the compiler of the Vedas).
*   **Astrology/Horoscopy** <note>original: Horā</note> — This term specifically refers to the branch of astrology dealing with birth charts and the predictive analysis of time.
*   **Treatise** <note>original: Śāstram</note> — This indicates that the work is a systematic, authoritative body of scientific and spiritual knowledge.

The title presented on this cover identifies the work as the **Great Parashara Treatise on Astrology** <note>original Sanskrit: Bṛhat Pārāśara Horāśāstra</note>. This text is considered the "bible" of <term>Indian Astrology</term> <note>original: Jyotiṣa</note>, serving as the primary source for the system of calculation and interpretation used throughout the Indian subcontinent for centuries.

The title is composed of several significant Sanskrit components:

*   **Great** <note>original: Bṛhat</note> — This prefix signals that the work is an expansive or "great" compilation, distinguishing it from smaller or "minor" <note>original: Laghu</note> summaries of the same astrological system.
*   **Of Parashara** <note>original: Pārāśara</note> — The work is attributed to the Sage Parashara, a legendary figure in Vedic literature who is said to have received the secrets of the planets and stars from the creator deity and passed them down to humanity.
*   **Astrology** <note>original: Horā</note> — This term specifically refers to the science of time and horoscopy. Ancient commentators often explained this word as being derived from the Sanskrit word for a "full day and night" <note>original: ahorātra</note>, specifically the portion dealing with the influence of the planets on human life.
*   **Treatise** <note>original: Śāstra</note> — This word indicates an authoritative body of knowledge, a science, or a sacred scripture that provides rules and guidance.

The physical condition of the manuscript, with its red cloth binding and pasted paper label, is typical of North Indian manuscript production in the 19th and early 20th centuries.

*   **Of Parashara** <note>original: Pārāśara</note> — The work is attributed to the Sage Parashara, a legendary figure in Vedic literature who is said to have received the secrets of the planets and stars from the creator deity and passed them down to humanity.
*   **Astrology** <note>original: Horā</note> — This term specifically refers to the science of time and horoscopy. Ancient commentators often explained this word as being derived from the Sanskrit word for a "full day and night" <note>original: ahorātra</note>, specifically the portion dealing with the influence of the planets on human life.
*   **Treatise** <note>original: Śāstra</note> — This word indicates an authoritative body of knowledge, a science, or a sacred scripture that provides rules and guidelines for a specific field of study.

<insert>
# The Great Parashara-
# Science of Horoscopy.
</insert>

This title label identifies the work as the **Great Parashara Science of Horoscopy** <note>original: Bṛhat Pārāśara Horā Śāstram</note>. In the tradition of <term>Indian Astrology</term> <note>original: Jyotiṣa; literally "the science of light"</note>, this text is considered the foundational and most authoritative treatise for calculating and interpreting planetary influences.

The title is composed of four specific terms:

*   **Great** <note>original: Bṛhat</note> — Signifying an expansive or primary version of the text.
*   **Of Parashara** <note>original: Pārāśara</note> — Attributed to the ancient Sage Parashara, a legendary figure in Vedic wisdom and father of the sage Vyasa.
*   **Horoscopy** <note>original: Horā</note> — The branch of astrology dealing specifically with time, the rising sign, and the casting of birth charts.
*   **Science or Treatise** <note>original: Śāstram</note> — A term used for a systematic body of technical or sacred knowledge.

<margin>The text is framed by a decorative printed border featuring repeating floral and geometric patterns, typical of traditional manuscript labels from the late 19th or early 20th century.</margin>

<note>This manuscript is part of the collection at the Shri Krishna Museum in Kurukshetra, digitized by eGangotri.</note>

# PARASHARA’S ASTROLOGY.

<note>original: "Bṛhatpārāśarahorā-śāstram" — <term>Bṛhat</term> translates to "Great" or "Vast," indicating the comprehensive nature of this version; <term>Pārāśara</term> refers to the legendary Sage Parashara, the grandfather of the epic poet Vyasa and the attributed author; <term>Horā</term> refers to the study of time and natal astrology; and <term>Śāstra</term> denotes a scientific, systematic, or sacred treatise of authoritative knowledge.</note>

<note>The term <term>Jyotisha</term> refers to the traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology. The "Hora Shastra" is the specific branch of this science focused on the interpretation of birth charts to understand human destiny.</note>

### Technical Vocabulary

**The Great Treatise on Astrology by Parashara** (<term>Bṛhat Pārāśara Horā Śāstra</term>): Considered the most comprehensive and authoritative source of <term>Jyotisha</term> (Indian astrology).

**Astrology/Astronomy** (<term>Jyotisha</term>): From the Sanskrit root meaning "light" or "heavenly body," it refers to the traditional Hindu system of observing the stars and planets.

**Horoscopy/Time** (<term>Hora</term>): A branch of astrology focusing on the interpretation of planetary positions at the time of birth or a specific event; the word is also historically linked to the Greek word for "hour."

### Technical Vocabulary

**The Great Treatise on Parashara’s Astrology** (<term>Bṛhat Pārāśara Horā Śāstra</term>): Considered the most comprehensive and authoritative source of <term>Jyotisha</term> (Indian astrology), this work is attributed to the Vedic sage Parashara. It serves as the primary manual for practitioners of the craft.

**Astrology/Astronomy** (<term>Jyotisha</term>): Derived from the Sanskrit root for "light" or "heavenly body," it refers to the traditional Hindu system of observing stars and planets for time-keeping, calendar construction, and divination.

**Horoscopy/Time** (<term>Hora</term>): A specific branch of astrology focusing on the interpretation of planetary positions at the time of birth or a specific event. Linguistically, it is related to the English word "hour," both descending from roots meaning a period of time.

### Technical Vocabulary

**The Great Treatise on Parashara’s Astrology** (<term>Bṛhat Pārāśara Horā Śāstra</term>): This work is the primary pillar of Indian natal astrology. Traditionally written as a series of instructions from the sage Parashara to his student Maitreya, it details the complex mathematical systems used to calculate planetary strength and interpret the influence of the stars on human life.

### Technical Vocabulary

**The Great Treatise on Parashara’s Astrology** (<term>Bṛhat Pārāśara Horā Śāstra: The primary foundational text of Indian astrology</term>): This is the most comprehensive and respected work in the field of <term>Jyotisha</term>. **The Great Treatise on Parashara’s Astrology** (<term>Bṛhat Pārāśara Horā Śāstra: The most authoritative and comprehensive compendium of Indian predictive astrology.</term>): This text is the cornerstone of <term>Jyotisha</term> (traditional Indian astronomy and astrology, literally "the science of light"). Traditionally attributed to the sage <term>Parashara</term>—the grandfather of the legendary poet Vyasa—the work is structured as a dialogue between the sage and his disciple Maitreya. It covers everything from the creation of the universe and the nature of the planets to the calculation of life span and the effects of various planetary combinations.

The **<term>Brihat Parashara Hora Shastra</term>** <note>original: "बृहत्पाराशरहोराशास्त्रम्"</note> is considered the foundational "bible" of **<term>Vedic Astrology</term>** <note>original: "Jyotisha," the traditional Hindu system of astronomy and astrology</note>. The term *Bṛhat* means "Great" or "Extensive," while *Horā* refers to the study of time and horoscopes. This specific edition features a label typical of printed books from the colonial era in India, often bound for library collections.</note>

->The title is printed on a rectangular cream-colored paper label, affixed to the center of a red textured cloth book cover. <note>The title identifies this work as the **<term>Bṛhat Pārāśara Horāśāstra</term>**, the foundational "Great Treatise" of Indian horoscopic astrology. In this context, **<term>Bṛhat</term>** means "great" or "vast," referring to the encyclopedic nature of the work. **<term>Pārāśara</term>** refers to the ancient sage Parāśara, the traditional author and a central figure in Vedic genealogy. **<term>Horā</term>** is a technical term derived from the Greek *hōra* (hour), referring to the study of time and planetary hours, and **<term>Śāstra</term>** denotes a systematic, authoritative science or scripture.</note>

# Science of Astrology

<note>original: "बृहत्पाराशरहोरा-शास्त्रम्" (Bṛhat Pārāśara Horā-Śāstram)</note>

---

<note>The title identifies this work as the **<term>Bṛhat Pārāśara Horāśāstra</term>**, which is considered the foundational and most authoritative text of Indian horoscopic astrology (<term>Jyotiṣa</term>). The term **<term>Bṛhat</term>** means "great" or "extensive," denoting the comprehensive nature of this version. **<term>Pārāśara</term>** refers to the ancient sage Parāśara, who is traditionally credited as the author. **<term>Horā</term>** specifically refers to the branch of astrology dealing with individual horoscopes and the passage of time, while **<term>Śāstra</term>** indicates a formal, scientific treatise or sacred body of knowledge.</note>

The <term>Bṛhat Pārāśara Horā Śāstra</term> is the foundational and most comprehensive treatise in the field of <term>Jyotiṣa</term> (Indian astrology). The title translates to the "Great" (<term>Bṛhat</term>) scientific work (<term>Śāstra</term>) on horoscopy and time-keeping (<term>Horā</term>) attributed to the sage <term>Parāśara</term>. 

In the Vedic tradition, <term>Parāśara</term> is a highly revered <term>Rishi</term> (an inspired seer or sage) and is traditionally identified as the father of Vyāsa, the legendary author of the Mahabharata. This text is the cornerstone of the "Parāśari" system, which remains the most widely practiced methodology of predictive astrology in India today.
</note>

<note>
**Physical Description and Condition:** 
The manuscript is bound in a red textured cloth cover. Centered on the front is a cream-colored paper label containing the title in Devanagari script. The label is framed by a decorative border of repeating floral motifs, a common aesthetic choice for 19th and early 20th-century Indian publications. 

The artifact shows signs of age: the paper label is torn at the top right corner, and the red cloth possesses several dark stains—likely ink—located just below the title. Digital watermarks at the bottom indicate the item is part of the archival collection at the Shri Krishna Museum, Kurukshetra, and was digitized by eGangotri.
</note>

# The Great Compendium of Parāśara’s 
# Astrological Science

<note>original: "बृहत्पाराशरहोरा-शास्त्रम्" (Bṛhatpārāśarahorā-śāstram)</note>

<note>
**Visual Description:** 
The title is printed on a rectangular paper label pasted onto the center of a red, textured book cover. The label is adorned with a simple decorative floral border. There is visible staining on the lower portion of the cover, and the label itself shows a small tear in the top right corner, indicating its age and history of use.
</note>

<note>
**Interpretive Context:**
The *Bṛhat Pārāśara Horā Śāstra* is considered the foundational "bible" of <term>Jyotiṣa</term> (Vedic astrology). This monumental work is traditionally attributed to the Sage Parāśara, the grandson of Vasiṣṭha and father of Vyāsa (the compiler of the Vedas). It is structured as a dialogue where the sage answers the inquiries of his disciple, Maitreya, regarding the laws of the cosmos and their influence on human life.

- <term>Bṛhat</term>: Meaning "Great" or "Vast," this prefix indicates that this version is a comprehensive and authoritative edition of the teachings.
- <term>Pārāśara</term>: Refers to the legendary sage Parāśara, the primary authority on natal astrology in the Hindu tradition.
- <term>Horā</term>: A technical term for the branch of astrology focused on birth charts and the predictive measurement of time. It is traditionally said to be derived from the Sanskrit word *ahorātra* (day and night).
- <term>Śāstra</term>: A scientific, systematic, or sacred treatise.
</note>

Attributed to the sage Parāśara—traditionally identified as the father of Vyāsa, the author of the Mahabharata—it is the most comprehensive ancient Sanskrit treatise on natal astrology. The term <term>Horā</term> specifically refers to the branch of astrology dealing with the prediction of future events based on the time of birth, while <term>Śāstra</term> denotes a formal scientific or instructional compendium.
</note>

# The Great Compendium of Parāśara’s
# Astrological Science.

<note>original: "बृहत्पाराशरहोरा-शास्त्रम्" (Bṛhatpārāśarahorā-śāstram)</note>

<note>
**Condition Report:**
The title label, which is printed on paper and affixed to the volume, is partially torn at the top right corner. The red cover of the book shows dark staining below the label area. 
</note>

<note>
**Visual and Decorative Description:**
The title is framed by a decorative border featuring a repeating geometric and floral pattern. This style of ornamentation was common for title labels in Indian book production during the 19th and early 20th centuries.
</note>

<note>
**Interpretive Context:**
This work, the *Bṛhat Pārāśara Horā Śāstra*, is considered the most authoritative and comprehensive manual of <term>Jyotiṣa</term> (traditional Indian astrology). It is traditionally attributed to the sage Parāśara. The title breaks down as follows: *Bṛhat* (Great/Extensive), *Pārāśara* (belonging to the sage Parāśara), <term>Horā</term> (the study of time and natal astrology), and <term>Śāstra</term> (a formal scientific treatise or compendium).
</note>

<note>

The decorative floral border on the paper label is characteristic of 19th or early 20th-century Indian printing. While the content is ancient, this physical volume represents a period when traditional palm-leaf or hand-written manuscripts were being transition into printed books for wider use by practicing astrologers and scholars.
</note>

<note>
**Interpretive Context:**
This title identifies the work as the foundational authority on <term>Jyotiṣa</term>—the ancient science of light and time, commonly known as Indian astrology. This specific text is traditionally attributed to the sage Parāśara, a towering figure in the Vedic tradition who is also credited as the father of Vyāsa, the compiler of the Vedas.

The title is composed of four key Sanskrit elements:
1. **Great** (*Bṛhat*): Signifies that this is a comprehensive, expanded, or "major" collection of astrological knowledge.
2. **Of Parāśara** (*Pārāśara*): Credits the lineage of the teachings to the sage Parāśara, establishing its authoritative status.
3. <term>Horā</term>: A technical term (often linked to the Sanskrit word *ahorātra*, meaning "day and night") referring to the specific branch of astrology concerned with natal charts, individual destiny, and the passage of hours.
4. <term>Śāstra</term>: A formal scientific treatise, manual, or sacred rule-book that provides structured knowledge.
</note>

<note>
**Museum Note on the Edition:**
The decorative floral border on the paper label is characteristic of 19th or early 20th-century Indian printing styles. While the wisdom contained within is ancient, this physical volume represents a historical period when traditional palm-leaf or hand-written manuscripts were being transitioned into printed books to make them more accessible to practicing astrologers and scholars.
</note>

The title is displayed on a central paper label pasted onto a red, textured book cover. This label is framed by a decorative woodcut border featuring repeating floral and geometric patterns, a common design in Indian printing during the late 19th and early 20th centuries. 

The manuscript shows physical signs of age and significant use: 
* <unclear>The upper right corner of the paper label is torn.</unclear>

This work is the **Great Compendium of Parāśara’s Science of Time**, the foundational pillar of <term>Jyotiṣa</term>—the ancient Indian system of astronomy and astrology. The text is traditionally attributed to the sage Parāśara, a central figure in Vedic literature.

The title contains several specialized terms:
*   **Great** (*Bṛhat*): Denotes that this is a comprehensive and expanded version of the knowledge.
*   **Parāśara**: The name of the lineage-holder and sage credited with the revelation of these astrological principles.
*   <term>Horā</term>: A technical term for the branch of astrology focused on the passage of hours, natal charts, and individual destiny. It is traditionally linked to the Sanskrit word for "day and night" (*ahorātra*).
*   <term>Śāstra</term>: A formal scientific treatise, sacred rule-book, or authoritative manual.

# The Great Compendium of Parāśara’s
# Science of Time.

<note>original: "बृहत्पाराशरहोरा-शास्त्रम्" (Bṛhat Pārāśara Horā-śāstram)</note>

This page features the central title label for the **Great Compendium of Parāśara’s Science of Time**, the most significant and foundational work in the tradition of <term>Jyotiṣa</term>—the ancient Indian science of light, which encompasses both astronomy and astrology.

The work is attributed to the venerable sage Parāśara, who is a central figure in the lineage of Vedic wisdom. The title translates as follows:

*   **Great** (*Bṛhat*): Indicates that this is a comprehensive, large-scale, and expanded version of the astrological teachings.

*   **Great** (*Bṛhat*): Indicates that this is the expanded, most complete version of these celestial teachings.

*   **Horoscopy** (*Horā*): The specific study of birth charts and the influence of time on human life. <note>The term *Horā* is etymologically linked to the Sanskrit word *Ahorātra*, meaning "day and night," representing the full cycle of time.</note>

<insert>
## The Great Science of Parāśara’s
## Horoscopy.
</insert>

<meta>CC-0 Shri Krishna Museum, Kurukshetra. Digitized by eGangotri</meta>

This label identifies the manuscript as the <term>Bṛhat Parāśara Horā Śāstra</term> <note>original Sanskrit: "बृहत्पाराशरहोराशास्त्रम्" (Bṛhatpārāśarahorāśāstram)</note>. 

This work is considered the foundational treatise of <term>Jyotiṣa</term> <note>the traditional Hindu system of astrology and astronomy</note>. It is traditionally attributed to the sage Parāśara, a prominent figure in Vedic literature who is also known as the father of Vyāsa, the narrator of the *Mahābhārata*.

The title provides a clear description of the book's contents through four key terms:
*   **Great** (*Bṛhat*): Denotes that this is a comprehensive or "major" version of the teachings.
*   **Parāśara**: The name of the ancient seer (*Rishi*) to whom these astrological secrets were revealed.
*   **Horoscopy** (*Horā*): Referring to the branch of astrology dealing with birth charts, the rising sign, and the effects of time on human life.
*   **Science** (*Śāstra*): A term for an authoritative manual, systematic treatise, or body of knowledge.

The label is framed by a decorative repeating border. This style of ornamentation was typical for printed labels used by publishers and libraries in India during the late 19th and early 20th centuries, suggesting the period when this specific volume was bound or cataloged.

## The Great Compendium of Parāśara’s
## Science of Horoscopy.

This label identifies the manuscript as the <term>Bṛhat Parāśara Horā Śāstra</term> <note>original Sanskrit: "बृहत्पाराशरहोराशास्त्रम्" (Bṛhatpārāśarahorāśāstram)</note>. 

The work is the foundational text of <term>Jyotiṣa</term> <note>the traditional Hindu system of astrology and astronomy</note>. It is traditionally attributed to the sage Parāśara, a revered figure in ancient Indian literature and the father of Vyāsa, the legendary author of the *Mahābhārata*.

The title is composed of four descriptive Sanskrit terms:
*   **Great** (*Bṛhat*): Indicates that this is an extensive or "major" version of the teachings.
*   **Parāśara**: The name of the ancient seer or *Rishi* who is said to have received these secrets from the creator god, Brahma.
*   **Horoscopy** (*Horā*): Derived from the Sanskrit word for the "rising sign," this refers to the branch of astrology focused on birth charts and the influence of time on human destiny.
*   **Science** (*Śāstra*): Refers to an authoritative, systematic treatise or manual of knowledge.

# The Great Compendium of Parāśara’s
# Science of Horoscopy.

<note>original Sanskrit: "बृहत्पाराशरहोरा-शास्त्रम्" (Bṛhatpārāśarahorā-śāstram)</note>

This label identifies the volume as the <term>Bṛhat Parāśara Horā Śāstra</term>, the preeminent foundational text of <term>Jyotiṣa</term> <note>the traditional Hindu system of astrology and astronomy</note>. This "Great" (<italic>Bṛhat</italic>) treatise is traditionally attributed to the ancient sage Parāśara, a revered figure who is said to have received the secrets of the cosmos from the creator and then transmitted them to his disciple, Maitreya.

The title is composed of four essential elements:
*   **Great** (*Bṛhat*): Denotes that this is a comprehensive and major version of the teachings.
*   **Parāśara**: The name of the semi-legendary <term>Rishi</term> <note>an inspired sage or seer</note> to whom the work is credited.
*   **Horoscopy** (*Horā*): A term derived from the Sanskrit word for the "rising sign" or the passage of time, focusing on birth charts and human destiny.
*   **Science** (*Śāstra*): Refers to a systematic, authoritative body of knowledge or a sacred manual.

<margin>The paper label is damaged with a visible tear in the upper right corner.</margin>

# The Great Compendium of Parāśara’s
# Science of Horoscopy.

<note>original Sanskrit: वृहत्पाराशरहोरा-शास्त्रम् (Bṛhatpārāśarahorā-śāstram)</note>

This label identifies the volume as the <term>Bṛhat Parāśara Horā Śāstra</term>. In the world of Indian scholarship, this is the foundational and most authoritative text of <term>Jyotiṣa</term> <note>the traditional Hindu system of astrology and astronomy</note>. This "Great" (*Bṛhat*) treatise is traditionally attributed to the ancient sage Parāśara, a revered <term>Rishi</term> <note>an inspired sage or seer</note> who is said to have lived during the Vedic period.

The title is composed of four essential concepts:
*   **Great** (*Bṛhat*): Signifies that this is the comprehensive or major version of the astrological teachings, distinguishing it from shorter or later summaries.
*   **Parāśara**: The name of the legendary sage who serves as the primary authority and narrator of the text.
*   **Horoscopy** (*Horā*): A technical term in Sanskrit—possibly related to the Greek *hōra*—referring to the study of time, particularly the interpretation of the "rising sign" at the moment of birth.
*   **Science** (*Śāstra*): Denotes a systematic, authoritative body of knowledge, a manual, or a sacred treatise.

<margin>The central title is framed by a decorative border of repeating floral and geometric patterns. This style of border is characteristic of printed book labels produced in India during the late 19th or early 20th centuries.</margin>

# The Great Treatise on 
# Parāśara’s Horoscopy

<margin>The central title label is framed by a decorative woodcut border with repeating floral and geometric patterns. This style is characteristic of early printed labels or high-quality manuscript identification tags in Northern India.</margin>

<insert><unclear>L.B.</unclear> <unclear>7</unclear></insert> <note>These handwritten markings are likely library shelf-marks or administrative accession numbers added by the museum or a previous collector.</note>

This central label identifies the volume as the <term>Bṛhat Parāśara Horā Śāstra</term> <note>original Sanskrit: बृहत्पाराशरहोराशास्त्रम्</note>. In the tradition of Indian scholarship, this is considered the foundational and most authoritative text of <term>Jyotiṣa</term> <note>the traditional Hindu system of astrology and astronomy</note>. This "Great" (*Bṛhat*) treatise is traditionally attributed to the ancient sage <term>Parāśara</term>, a revered <term>Rishi</term> <note>an inspired sage or seer</note> who is known in Vedic tradition as the father of Vyāsa, the legendary author of the *Mahābhārata*.

The title is composed of four essential concepts:

*   **Great** (*Bṛhat*): Signifies that this is the comprehensive or major version of these astrological teachings, distinguishing it from shorter or condensed versions that circulated later.
*   **Parāśara**: The name of the legendary sage who serves as the primary authority and narrator of the text, presenting the knowledge as a dialogue.
*   **Horoscopy** (*Horā*): A technical term in Indian astrology specifically dealing with predictive astrology and birth charts. It is historically related to the Greek word for hour <note>original: hōra / ὥρα</note>, reflecting the ancient exchange of astronomical ideas between the Mediterranean and India.
*   **Treatise** (*Śāstra*): A word denoting a systematic body of knowledge, science, or a sacred text that provides instruction and authority on a specific subject.

# The Great Compendium of Parāśara’s-
# Astrology.

<note>original: "Bṛhat Pārāśara Horā-śāstram"</note>

This title identifies the manuscript as the **Great Treatise on Astrology by Parāśara**. Within the tradition of <term>Jyotish</term> <note>the traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology, literally meaning 'the science of light'</note>, this is considered the most comprehensive and authoritative source text.

The title is broken down as follows:
*   **Great** <note>original: Bṛhat</note>: Indicates that this is the expanded or "large" version of the collected teachings.

The title consists of the following technical terms:
*   **Great** <note>original: Bṛhat</note>: Indicates that this is the expanded or comprehensive version of the teachings.

This title page introduces the **Great Compendium of Parāśara’s Science of Astrology**, the foundational text of <term>Jyotisha</term> <note>the traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology, literally "the science of light"</note>. This work is regarded as the most authoritative and comprehensive manual for calculating planetary positions and interpreting their influence on human life.

The title is composed of four distinct Sanskrit elements:

*   **Great** <note>original: Bṛhat</note>: This prefix indicates that the volume is an expansive and definitive version of the astrological traditions.
*   **Parāśara’s**: Named for the ancient Vedic sage Parāśara, the father of Vyāsa. He is traditionally credited with receiving this celestial knowledge and passing it down to his disciple Maitreya.
*   **Science of Astrology** <note>original: Horā</note>: A specific branch of <term>Jyotisha</term> dealing with horoscopy and the measurement of time. <note>The term "horā" is linguistically linked to the Greek "hōra," meaning hour or season.</note>
*   **Sacred Treatise** <note>original: Śāstram</note>: A term denoting a work of specialized, authoritative knowledge or a sacred scripture.

The layout of the label, with its ornate borders, is characteristic of printed or hand-stamped book labels from the late 19th or early 20th century in India, marking this as a relatively modern preservation of an ancient oral and manuscript tradition.

This manuscript cover presents the title of one of the most significant works in the history of Indian science. The **Great Compendium of Parāśara’s Science of Astrology** is the primary authority for <term>Jyotish</term> <note>the traditional Indian system of astrology and astronomy, literally "the science of light"</note>. 

The title consists of four key components:

*   **Great** <note>original: Bṛhat</note>: This indicates the comprehensive and expansive nature of the work compared to shorter manuals.
*   **Parāśara’s**: Named after the Vedic sage Parāśara, who is traditionally considered the author and the father of Vyasa (the compiler of the Vedas).
*   **Science of Astrology** <note>original: Horā</note>: This specifically refers to horoscopic astrology—the study of the rise and fall of signs and the measurement of time.
*   **Treatise** <note>original: Śāstram</note>: Denotes a formal, authoritative system of knowledge or sacred scripture.

The label is set within a decorative floral border, a style common in 19th and early 20th-century Indian publications and manuscript bindings. The red cloth cover and the paper label reflect the preservation methods used by traditional libraries and collectors in North India.

<summary>This page is the title cover of the Bṛhat Parāśara Horā Śāstra, the most authoritative classical treatise on Vedic astrology attributed to the sage Parāśara.</summary>

*   **Treatise** <note>original: "Śāstram"</note>: This denotes a formal system of knowledge, a scientific manual, or a sacred scripture that provides a disciplined methodology.

In the tradition of <term>Jyotisha</term> <note>The traditional Indian system of astrology and astronomy, literally meaning the "science of light" or "heavenly bodies." It encompasses both mathematical astronomy and predictive astrology.</note>, this work is considered the foundational authority for all subsequent predictive practices.

The title is composed of several significant elements:

*   **The Great Compendium of Parāśara** <note>original Sanskrit: "Bṛhat-pārāśara"</note>: This indicates that the work is an expansive or "great" (*Bṛhat*) collection of teachings attributed to the Vedic sage Parāśara. In tradition, Parāśara is a revered figure, often identified as the father of Vyāsa, the narrator of the *Mahābhārata*.
*   **The Science of Astrology** <note>original Sanskrit: "Horā-śāstram"</note>: This term denotes a systematic treatise (<term>shastra</term> <note>A rule, command, or treatise; a specialized field of knowledge.</note>) concerning <term>Hora</term>. While often translated as "horoscopy," <term>Hora</term> refers more broadly to the study of time and the influence of the planets on human destiny.

->The label’s ornate floral woodcut border and the use of the Devanagari script are typical of high-quality manuscript labels from the late 19th or early 20th centuries.<-

## The Great Compendium of Parāśara’s—
## Science of Horoscopy.

<term>The Great Compendium of Parāśara’s Science of Horoscopy</term> <note>original Sanskrit: Bṛhatpārāśarahorā-śāstram</note> is the most significant and comprehensive foundational text of <term>Jyotisha</term> <note>the traditional Indian system of astrology and astronomy</note>. This work is categorized as a <term>Sastra</term> <note>an authoritative scientific or religious treatise</note>, implying it is not merely a guide but a systematic study of the laws governing time and celestial influence.

The title contains three key elements:
1. **Bṛhat**: Meaning "great," "large," or "expanded," indicating that this is the definitive, comprehensive version of these teachings.
2. **Parāśara**: The name of the ancient sage to whom the work is traditionally attributed. In Indian tradition, Parāśara is a foundational figure in intellectual history, often identified as the father of Vyāsa (the compiler of the Vedas).
3. **Horā**: A term derived from the Greek *hōra* or the Sanskrit *ahorātra* (day and night), specifically referring to the branch of astrology focused on natal charts and the prediction of human affairs based on the time of birth.

->[The book cover features a red textured binding. Centered on the front is a rectangular paper label containing the title in Devanagari script, surrounded by a decorative border of repeating geometric and floral patterns. The upper right corner of the label shows slight wear and tearing.]<-

This specific volume represents the core curriculum for practitioners of <term>Vedic Astrology</term>. It outlines the complex mathematics required to calculate planetary positions and the interpretive frameworks used to understand the "karmic map" of an individual's life.

# The Great Compendium of Parashara’s-
# Astrological Science.

<term>The Great Compendium of Parashara’s Horoscopic Science (Bṛhat Parāśara Horāśāstra)</term>: The foundational text of <term>Jyotisha</term> <note>traditional Indian astronomy and astrology</note>. It is written in <term>Sanskrit</term>, the ancient liturgical and scholarly language of India.

->The title label, printed on paper with a decorative floral and geometric border, is pasted onto the center of the book's red textured cover. This style of border is typical for labels produced in the 19th or early 20th century. The label shows signs of wear and age, with a tear at the top-right corner and dark ink stains on the fabric below.<-

<term>The Great Compendium (Bṛhat)</term>: This prefix literally means "vast," "great," or "extended." It indicates that this version is a comprehensive edition of the teachings, distinguishing it from shorter or abridged versions. <note>original Sanskrit: "बृहत्" (Bṛhat)</note>

<term>Parashara (Pārāśara)</term>: Pertaining to the Sage Parashara. In Indian tradition, Parashara is a semi-divine seer (Rishi), the grandson of Vashistha, and the traditional father of the main system of horoscopic astrology used today. <note>original Sanskrit: "पाराशर" (Pārāśara)</note>

<term>Astrological Science (Horā-Śāstra)</term>: A technical compound where *Horā* refers to "horoscopy" or the study of time, and *Śāstra* refers to a scientific treatise or sacred body of knowledge. <note>original Sanskrit: "होराशास्त्र" (Horā-śāstra)</note>

# The Great Compendium of Parashara’s-
# Astrological Science.

->The red book cover features a rectangular paper label with a decorative floral and geometric border. The label, though showing signs of age with a tear in the upper right corner and some minor staining, clearly displays the title. This style of label is characteristic of early modern South Asian book production. At the very bottom of the page, a digital mark indicates that the document was digitized by eGangotri for the Shri Krishna Museum, Kurukshetra.<-

The title presented here is the <term>Brihat Parashara Hora Shastra</term> <note>original Sanskrit: "बृहत्पाराशरहोराशास्त्रम्"</note>, the foundational text of <term>Jyotisha</term> <note>the traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology</note>. It is recorded in <term>Sanskrit</term>, the classical language of Indian scholarship and liturgy.

<term>The Great Compendium (Bṛhat)</term>: This prefix literally means "vast," "great," or "extended." It indicates that this version is a comprehensive edition of the teachings, distinguishing it from shorter or abridged versions. <note>original Sanskrit: "बृहत्"</note>

<term>Parashara (Pārāśara)</term>: Pertaining to the Sage Parashara. In Indian tradition, Parashara is a semi-divine seer (Rishi), the grandson of Vashistha, and the traditional father of the main system of horoscopic astrology used today. <note>original Sanskrit: "पाराशर"</note>

<term>Astrological Science (Horā-Śāstra)</term>: A technical compound where *Horā* refers to "horoscopy" or the study of time, and *Śāstra* refers to a scientific treatise or sacred body of knowledge. <note>original Sanskrit: "होराशास्त्र"</note>
